Text: What is the most promising propulsion technology for theoretical manned Interstellar travel? What percentage of the speed of light could be theoretically reached? If I had to bet, I’d bet on the Bussard ramjet. Yes, I know it that there were studies questioning its feasibility. I read some of them. Still. The reason? It is the only approach I know of that a) does not rely on exotic physics, and b) does not require a spacecraft to carry absolutely insane quantities of propellant. A Bussard ramjet works by collecting interstellar hydrogen using a large, very powerful magnetic field, and then burning that hydrogen in a fusion engine. As such, a Bussard ramjet does not have a theoretical limit as to how close it can get to the vacuum speed of light, as it can accelerate forever. Much as I enjoy Star Trek, I am not keen on the concept of warp drives in the real universe. I mean, they look great on paper as theoretical solutions of Einstein’s field equations, but hey, I can also have theoretical solutions that involve closed timelike curves, and I have yet to meet Dr. Who with his lovely TARDIS. There is a world of a difference between building a mathematical construct of a universe that may be consistent with Einstein’s field equations, vs. taking this, one-and-only, universe in which we live, with ordinary matter in it, and bring that matter together in a configuration that creates a “warp field”. Call me small-minded but I do not think that is possible; not because of limits of technology, simply because warp drives, just like time machines, don’t exist in this universe. Same goes (even more so) for wormholes and other exotic solutions. What about super-efficient rockets? There we have a problem. Even if we have a maximum efficiency photon rocket powered by matter-antimatter annihilation, we still need absolutely insane quantities of fuel to accelerate a given spaceship to relativistic speeds. The rocket equation stands in our way: soon, when we calculate a round trip to a distant star, which we would like to execute within the lifetime of a human astronaut, we find that to accelerate our, say, 100-ton spaceship to the requisite speeds requires megatons of fuel. Do we really want to sit on top of megatons of antimatter, even if we knew how to manufacture antimatter in quantity, which we don’t? Is that ever going to be practical? And even if it is, once that spaceship runs out of fuel, it’s dead in space… whereas our Bussard ramjet only needs a small amount of residual fuel to be started, and then it starts collecting its own fuel again, with increasing efficiency as it accelerates. Of course things can change. New technologies may be invented. There may be new breakthroughs in theoretical physics that completely change its landscape. But in the here and now, I consider the ramjet the most promising approach, despite the spectacular technical challenges that might stand in its way. I don’t often use Quora’s AI-generated images anymore, but I admit I like this one. Nice ship! If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Text: I always read Victor Toth that the singularity is a moment in the future, not a point in place. What will happen to an observer falling into a black hole as he sees it for himself? Will he be crushed? To observers outside the event horizon of a black hole, never mind the singularity, the event horizon itself remains forever in the future, hidden from view by infinite time dilation. The way to think about it… imagine particles collapsing toward each other, accelerated by their mutual gravity. If no force pushes them back, eventually they would form a black hole. But when? Now imagine that these are not ordinary particles, but each and every one of them is a miniature spaceship equipped with a very powerful rocket. And suppose that each of these particles has a mind of its own. As they fall toward each other, perhaps one of the particles changes its mind at the last minute, last second, last picosecond, turns on its rocket and escapes. The point is, to you, the outside observer that last minute, last second, last picosecond might be the next day, the next year, the next five hundred trillion years. No matter how far into the future you go, you can never exclude the possibility that one of the infalling particles re-emerges, because in your reference frame, the event horizon has not yet formed! But you are asking what would happen to an infalling observer. Take one of those particles that is falling into the black hole. Let’s call this particle the observer. What would it see? Well, for starters, it’s surrounded by other particles, and above it, perhaps it still sees a clear view of space, with the distant stars. But the closer it gets to where the event horizon will form, the less sky it sees, because light from neighboring particles, even when it sets off in an almost vertical direction, would curve back down. The view “up” would become an ever narrower “tunnel”, until the tunnel disappears altogether, and the observer is just surrounded by other particles in all directions above and below. This happens at the moment the observer crosses the event horizon. When we look at the spacetime that this observer now finds itself in, it is actually much like the spacetime of cosmology: filled with matter (infalling particles) everywhere. From the observer’s viewpoint it will not be homogeneous (same everywhere) or isotropic (same in all directions) but that’s because the observer itself moves relative to the bulk of other particles. If the observer were to changes its trajectory, it might find itself in a homogeneous, isotropic, and collapsing mini-universe. Even without the trajectory change, it’s still a collapsing mini-universe, just not homogeneous and isotropic from the observer’s perspective. And the observer is doomed. This mini-universe only has a finite lifetime. It collapses, its density and temperature increasing beyond limit. The asymptotic final state is the singularity: a future, terminal moment in time that is not actually even part of this mini-universe. The existence of this mini-universe ends at that moment (it is “geodesically incomplete”). At least this is the case if the mini-universe has no net rotation. If it rotates, things get weirder and perhaps the observer might even avoid a terminal moment. We don’t really know: There have been several attempts to describe the interior of a rotating black hole solution, but no good solutions have been found, as far as I know. Anyhow, the important thing to remember is that relativity is about what different observers see. The singularity may be an unavoidable destiny for an infalling observer who has only a very short amount of time left, but to an observer outside the event horizon, it remains forever in the future. Text: Why is it challenging to comprehend quantum mechanics? Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty? Why is it challenging for a language model like GPT-4 to reason about geometry? The answer is simple: It doesn’t have the hardware to visualize geometry. It is forced to reason it out, step-by-step, in a process that is prone to mistakes. Our problem with quantum physics is similar. Our brain has wonderful hardware to visualize and intuit things in a classical universe. A universe in which quantum effects are averaged out, so what remains is basically geometry. And unlike GPT-4, our brain is wired to visualize geometry. But Nature doesn’t care. Nature doesn’t care about Einstein’s perspective either. The quantum world works differently, and our brains are not wired to intuit it. So like GPT-4 when it tries to reason about geometry, we have to do it step-by-step, in an error-prone, difficult process. Mind you, some of our attempts to “make sense” of quantum mechanics only made it worse, and personally, I list the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics among these. According to the Copenhagen interpretation, the present does not fully determine the state of a quantum system. This state is represented by a wavefunction that can be interpreted as a probability amplitude, which can be used to compute probabilities, but not certainties, when it comes to the outcome of future observations. Then, the act of observation, or “measurement” somehow magically “collapses” the wavefunction in a process that is not included in the equations of quantum physics; this collapse is instantaneous and applies everywhere even retroactively, as we replace one wavefunction with a different one. As to what a “measurement” is, and whether or not it can be done by an instrument, a cat, or if it requires a human, the Copenhagen interpretation remains silent about. Einstein was right in my view to be unsatisfied about this line of reasoning and the fact that it described the universe as fundamentally probabilistic. Unfortunately, he did not live long enough to see Bell’s theorem, which demonstrated beyond doubt that quantum physics is fundamentally nonlocal: that measurements are correlated even when they are so separated that no signal can pass between them, and that this correlation cannot be explained by “hidden variables” that the quantum system carries. If we fully embrace this nonlocality, all that probability stuff becomes unnecessary: The act of a future observation, the fact that the quantum system in the future is confined to an interaction with a camera, a cat or a human, constrains its wavefunction in the presence. No “collapse” needed and best of all, this nonlocality does not even violate causality: Much as we’d like to do so, it is not possible to use it to send signals from the future to the past. The constraints on the wavefunction imposed by its future interactions do not lead to observable consequences in the present. I have a feeling that Einstein would have embraced this direction. Alas, he died some nine years before Bell published his result. In any case, Bell’s theorem notwithstanding, quantum physics remains impossible to make sense of using our classical intuition. We need to do it the hard way, work it out, step-by-step, using the power of reason (expressed using the language of mathematics) as we lack the brain hardware to “see” quantum physics. Any attempt to “make sense” of quantum physics using our classical intuition is not only doomed to fail, it becomes an obstacle to understanding since quantum physics is manifestly not classical. Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty? Why is it challenging for a language model like GPT-4 to reason about geometry? The answer is simple: It doesn\u2019t have the hardware to visualize geometry. It is forced to reason it out, step-by-step, in a process that is prone to mistakes. Our problem with quantum physics is similar. Our brain has wonderful hardware to visualize and intuit things in a classical universe. A universe in which quantum effects are averaged out, so what remains is basically geometry. And unlike GPT-4, our brain is wired to visualize geometry. But Nature doesn\u2019t care. Nature doesn\u2019t care about Einstein\u2019s perspective either. The quantum world works differently, and our brains are not wired to intuit it. So like GPT-4 when it tries to reason about geometry, we have to do it step-by-step, in an error-prone, difficult process. Mind you, some of our attempts to \u201cmake sense\u201d of quantum mechanics only made it worse, and personally, I list the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics among these. According to the Copenhagen interpretation, the present does not fully determine the state of a quantum system. This state is represented by a wavefunction that can be interpreted as a probability amplitude, which can be used to compute probabilities, but not certainties, when it comes to the outcome of future observations. Then, the act of observation, or \u201cmeasurement\u201d somehow magically \u201ccollapses\u201d the wavefunction in a process that is not included in the equations of quantum physics; this collapse is instantaneous and applies everywhere even retroactively, as we replace one wavefunction with a different one. As to what a \u201cmeasurement\u201d is, and whether or not it can be done by an instrument, a cat, or if it requires a human, the Copenhagen interpretation remains silent about. Einstein was right in my view to be unsatisfied about this line of reasoning and the fact that it described the universe as fundamentally probabilistic. Unfortunately, he did not live long enough to see Bell\u2019s theorem, which demonstrated beyond doubt that quantum physics is fundamentally nonlocal: that measurements are correlated even when they are so separated that no signal can pass between them, and that this correlation cannot be explained by \u201chidden variables\u201d that the quantum system carries. No \u201ccollapse\u201d needed and best of all, this nonlocality does not even violate causality: Much as we\u2019d like to do so, it is not possible to use it to send signals from the future to the past. The constraints on the wavefunction imposed by its future interactions do not lead to observable consequences in the present. I have a feeling that Einstein would have embraced this direction. Alas, he died some nine years before Bell published his result. In any case, Bell\u2019s theorem notwithstanding, quantum physics remains impossible to make sense of using our classical intuition. We need to do it the hard way, work it out, step-by-step, using the power of reason (expressed using the language of mathematics) as we lack the brain hardware to \u201csee\u201d quantum physics. Any attempt to \u201cmake sense\u201d of quantum physics using our classical intuition is not only doomed to fail, it becomes an obstacle to understanding since quantum physics is manifestly not classical. Text: Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter? Absolutely. In the context of cosmological physics, matter and antimatter are both “ordinary”, visible matter, made up of particles that interact with each other and with the electromagnetic field. Dark matter does not interact with the electromagnetic field (or if it does, it does so very, very, very weakly) and does not interact with normal matter (which includes antimatter). We don’t know what dark matter is (we cannot even be sure that it exists) but if there is such a thing, this is its defining characteristic. In contrast, antimatter very much interacts with normal matter. So much so, that this is how we know that even distant regions of the visible universe are dominated by normal matter, not antimatter. How do we know? Matter is everywhere, there are hydrogen atoms even in intergalactic space. If there were, e.g., distant galaxy clusters made of antimatter, the boundary region between antimatter and normal matter regions would “glow” in the gamma ray part of the spectrum from the occasional matter-antimatter interactions. Granted, in the very low density intergalactic medium, such collisions would be infrequent, but on the other hand, the volumes are ginormous, and the resulting gamma ray background would be observable.

Text: If a human somehow managed to travel to the Sagittarius A* black hole, would they see exactly what the 2022 image shows us? Absolutely not unless their “eyes” are radio antennas. The images of Sgr A* are synthesized from radio astronomy observations. What they do show is a faint radio background from the accretion disk of Sgr A*, and on it, superimposed the “shadow” cast by the black hole’s photon sphere (the region around the black hole where gravity is powerful enough to force photons into unstable orbits). The published images are basically computer reconstructions based on a large number of observations made by a global network of radio telescopes. The reconstructions are also somewhat model-dependent: the images are reconstructed on the assumption that they came from an astrophysical black hole, whereas other models are shown the fit the data much less accurately. If you were to be close enough to Sgr A* to view it directly (naked eye or through a telescope), you might see something similar if there is a light source behind the black hole. That is to say, if the accretion disk emits sufficient amounts of visible light, you might see a similar shadow in the center, and for the same reason. But the appearance would be different, not to mention the color: the orange-ish color shown in the published images has nothing to do with physics (again, the actual observation was done by way of radio waves, not visible light), it’s basically an artistic choice. I try to avoid adding AI-generated images to my answers as, well, let’s face it, someone called them inane and they were not wrong. But I like this one. The AI must have “seen” the published Sgr A* images since it produced an image in the sky that bears some similarity in color and appearance. But what caught my eye is that field of… what are these, space poppies in the foreground? So, while begging the forgiveness of those who are not impressed by semi-relevant AI-generated imagery, allow me to indulge this time and keep this one. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Text: How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation? Distinguish between local measurements vs. measurements made from a distance. Suppose a photon zings by and you measure its speed: It’s 299,792,458 m/s. Other observers, at the same place where you are and at the same time, measuring the same photon, will measure the same speed even if those other observers are moving relative to you. However, when you look at distant photons, the situation changes. What you observe is subject to relativistic effects such as length contraction and time dilation. The speed you deduce can be anything. If you are on the surface of a neutron star and measure events far from that neutron star, you’ll see things unfold rapidly, as if you viewed them in fast forward mode. Conversely, if you are floating in deep space and check what happens on the surface of that neutron star, things will appear painfully slow, including photons. Text: What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Oh my, this is a hard question to answer... at least in a form suitable for a Quora answer. Let me try to keep it as simple as possible, which means necessarily skipping over some details, but still. You know what vectors are, right? Basically, quantities that have a magnitude and a direction. You may have learned to form inner products of vectors, but that's a misleading notion on its own right. The inner product is formed between a vector and a "covector". One way to think about it, perhaps, is that whereas a vector may be measuring a length and a direction, a covector is measuring the change of something along that length. So whereas vectors are measured using, say, meters or feet, covectors are measured using "inverse" units of length, i.e., meters or feet are now in the denominator. So say, a vector measures a length in a certain direction as 1 meter. Or 100 centimeters. Someone says that they have distributed marbles with a density of 10 marbles per meter. Or 0.1 marbles per centimeter. So now you form an inner product... between a 1-meter vector and the marble density of 10 marbles per meter. Multiply the two, and you get 10 marbles. Change the coordinate system from meters to centimeters: Now you have a 100-cm vector and 0.1 marbles per cm. Multiply the two and... again you get 10 marbles! The inner product between a vector and a covector yields a "scalar", a pure number that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system. This is important. So then, we can actually "define" a covector as the thing that maps a vector into a scalar by applying the inner product. What do you call a thing that maps not one but two vectors into a scalar? Wait, two vectors? Why would we want to do that? Well, how about characterizing how a force works on a surface. The force is a vector. The surface, a small surface element that is, can be characterized by a vector: its "normal" vector indicating its orientation and size. In continuum mechanics, we look at surface elements and the force acting on them. That force can be present due to pressure and stresses in the material. The point is, we need to relate these two vectors together... and the relationship is accomplished by introducing a thing called the "stress tensor", which can basically form an inner product with this pair of vectors. This also happens to be one of the earliest (early 19th century!) applications of tensors in physics. And this then allows us to generalize. If a covector maps a vector into a scalar, a covariant rank-N tensor can map N vectors into a scalar. Conversely, a vector can map a covector into a scalar; so a contravariant rank-N tensor can map N covectors into a scalar. And it is then easy to form "mixed index" tensors that map a collection of, say, N vectors and K covectors into a scalar. That's what tensors do: establish a relationship between vectors and covectors, mapping them into scalar quantities that do not depend on the choice of coordinate system in which the vectors are measured or expressed. Rank-2 tensors can be easily represented using matrices (though technically, it's only the rank-2 mixed index tensors, which map one vector and one covector into a scalar, that should be written as such, rows corresponding to the covariant, columns to the contravariant features of the tensor.) Higher-rank tensors are not that easy to represent as they require either multiple matrices or higher-domensional (cubic, etc.) structures which are not easy to put on paper. One of the wonderful things about tensors, however, is that they allow us to talk about physics without picking a specific coordinate system! If a vector V and a covector U form a scalar, say, V ⋅ U = 1 , that equation remains valid regardless of the coordinate system chosen. This allows us to distinguish physics (the actual things) from mathematics (the representation of those things) very cleanly. Going back to the inner product, we can of course calculate the inner product between two vectors if we have a corresponding rank-2 covariant tensor that we use to map the pair of vectors into a number. The "metric tensor" does this. The number, in this case, may be the length of the small difference between two near-identical vectors. This turns out to be an effective measure of the intrinsic geometry of the plane, of space, of spacetime. Normally, this "metric tensor" is just a generalization of the Pythagorean rule to calculate distances. But things get more complicated in general relativity, where the geometry of spacetime varies from place to place. So say, take a vector. Displace it so that it moves a tiny distance away, following a closed path, arriving back at its point of origin. So now you have a second vector (the direction of the displacement); a third vector (the direction the displaced vector follows when it arrives back at the point of origin); and a fourth vector (the final vector after arrival). The first and the fourth vector would be identical in Euclidean space. They are not in general relativity. The rank-4 tensor that relates these four vectors is the "Riemann curvature tensor", its value changing from point to point reflecting changing curvature. The relationship between this curvature tensor and the presence of matter amounts to the fundamental statement of general relativity, in the form of Einstein's field equations. Well, that's the gist of it. As I said, I glossed over many details. But hopefully at least it's a meaningful glimpse of the role of tensors in physics, relativity theory in particular. tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Oh my, this is a hard question to answer... at least in a form suitable for a Quora answer. Let me try to keep it as simple as possible, which means necessarily skipping over some details, but still. You know what vectors are, right? Basically, quantities that have a magnitude and a direction. You may have learned to form inner products of vectors, but that's a misleading notion on its own right. The inner product is formed between a vector and a \"covector\". One way to think about it, perhaps, is that whereas a vector may be measuring a length and a direction, a covector is measuring the change of something along that length. So whereas vectors are measured using, say, meters or feet, covectors are measured using \"inverse\" units of length, i.e., meters or feet are now in the denominator. So say, a vector measures a length in a certain direction as 1 meter. Or 100 centimeters. Someone says that they have distributed marbles with a density of 10 marbles per meter. Or 0.1 marbles per centimeter. So now you form an inner product... between a 1-meter vector and the marble density of 10 marbles per meter. Multiply the two, and you get 10 marbles. Change the coordinate system from meters to centimeters: Now you have a 100-cm vector and 0.1 marbles per cm. Multiply the two and... again you get 10 marbles! The inner product between a vector and a covector yields a \"scalar\", a pure number that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system. This is important. So then, we can actually \"define\" a covector as the thing that maps a vector into a scalar by applying the inner product. What do you call a thing that maps not one but two vectors into a scalar? Wait, two vectors? Why would we want to do that? Well, how about characterizing how a force works on a surface. The force is a vector. The surface, a small surface element that is, can be characterized by a vector: its \"normal\" vector indicating its orientation and size. In continuum mechanics, we look at surface elements and the force acting on them. That force can be present due to pressure and stresses in the material. The point is, we need to relate these two vectors together... and the relationship is accomplished by introducing a thing called the \"stress tensor\", which can basically form an inner product with this pair of vectors. This also happens to be one of the earliest (early 19th century!) applications of tensors in physics. And this then allows us to generalize. If a covector maps a vector into a scalar, a covariant rank-N tensor can map N vectors into a scalar. Conversely, a vector can map a covector into a scalar; so a contravariant rank-N tensor can map N covectors into a scalar. And it is then easy to form \"mixed index\" tensors that map a collection of, say, N vectors and K covectors into a scalar. That's what tensors do: establish a relationship between vectors and covectors, mapping them into scalar quantities that do not depend on the choice of coordinate system in which the vectors are measured or expressed. Rank-2 tensors can be easily represented using matrices (though technically, it's only the rank-2 mixed index tensors, which map one vector and one covector into a scalar, that should be written as such, rows corresponding to the covariant, columns to the contravariant features of the tensor.) Higher-rank tensors are not that easy to represent as they require either multiple matrices or higher-domensional (cubic, etc.) structures which are not easy to put on paper. One of the wonderful things about tensors, however, is that they allow us to talk about physics without picking a specific coordinate system! If a vector V and a covector U form a scalar, say, V \u22c5 U = 1 , that equation remains valid regardless of the coordinate system chosen. This allows us to distinguish physics (the actual things) from mathematics (the representation of those things) very cleanly. Going back to the inner product, we can of course calculate the inner product between two vectors if we have a corresponding rank-2 covariant tensor that we use to map the pair of vectors into a number. The \"metric tensor\" does this. The number, in this case, may be the length of the small difference between two near-identical vectors. This turns out to be an effective measure of the intrinsic geometry of the plane, of space, of spacetime. Normally, this \"metric tensor\" is just a generalization of the Pythagorean rule to calculate distances. But things get more complicated in general relativity, where the geometry of spacetime varies from place to place. So say, take a vector. Displace it so that it moves a tiny distance away, following a closed path, arriving back at its point of origin. So now you have a second vector (the direction of the displacement); a third vector (the direction the displaced vector follows when it arrives back at the point of origin); and a fourth vector (the final vector after arrival). The first and the fourth vector would be identical in Euclidean space. They are not in general relativity. The rank-4 tensor that relates these four vectors is the \"Riemann curvature tensor\", its value changing from point to point reflecting changing curvature. The relationship between this curvature tensor and the presence of matter amounts to the fundamental statement of general relativity, in the form of Einstein's field equations. Text: Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? Let me describe to you an imaginary journey into a classical black hole. ("Classical" in the sense that I am ignoring quantum effects, notably Hawking radiation, which might even prevent the black hole from forming in the first place. So let's say that you are not only in a very good spaceship, but you are also almost imprevious to extreme acceleration and extreme tidal forces. You hope into your spaceship, travel to the nearest collapsing sphere of matter that will ultimately form a black hole, and choose a trajectory that will end up in the black hole as well. If the collapsing matter has negligible pressure, its collapse will not be slowed down by any means. Yet to those on the outside, the process of the collapse will appear to slow as the cloud gets close to becoming a black hole. That is because of extreme gravitational time dilation: anything that happens near this collapsing cloud of matter will appear in slow motion to anyone far away. Not to you though. You will find that you will approach the surface of this collapsing cloud, but you won't quite be able to catch up with it. Meanwhile, however, as the gravitational field gets stronger, you will notice that what was a spherical surface below now appears to "curl up" on the sides. That is because of the gravitational deflection of light: many light rays that start off going upward will be bent downward, so they will appear to hit your eyeball from above! What was one a surface below begins to form a wall around you, and soon enough, it will feel like you are in a vertical tunnel, or well, its opening rapidly closing above you. Suppose you chicken out at the very last split second, punch a button, and with your Extremely Powerful Rocket [tm] you escape. Much to your surprise, you'll find that what has taken only a few seconds by your reckoning took a year outside. Or a thousand years. Or a quintillion years. This is why those on the outside can never be sure that the black hole even forms; no matter how long they wait, there's a chance that you re-emerge. It's only a question of how close you cut it before punching out. But what if you don't? Well, there will be a moment when the matter above your head closes up. There is no opening anymore. No walls really, either, as this is also the moment when you caught up with all the collapsing matter after all, so now you are inside the cloud. Inside a homogeneous (same everywhere) isotropic (no preferred direction) cloud of matter that forms a collapsing mini-universe, in which you are trapped. The moment when this happened is the event horizon. NOT a place. Not a location to which you can return. A moment — now a moment in the past — of time. So without a time machine, you are doomed. This mini-universe is a collapsing universe, the exact opposite of the kind of universe we seem to live in, outside of the black hole. Second by second, minute by minute it becomes denser. (Or millisecond by millisecond, if the collapsing cloud weighed "only" as much as, say, three times the mass of our Sun, or a million times the mass of the Earth.) Did I say same everywhere? Yes, I did. I meant it. There is no center, no edge of this cloud. This entire self-enclosed mini-universe is filled with matter everywhere. And you have very little time left. And perhaps that's when you recall something that you may have heard before in the past: The so-called "singularity" is not some center either. Rather, it is the moment in time when density, pressure, temperature, etc., everything in this mini-universe diverges, becomes infinite. The mini-universe ceases to exist (it's called geodesic incompleteness). Along with you, of course. Think this scenario through and now contemplate if it is even meaningful to talk about "destroying" a black hole. What exactly would that "destruction" do? Remember, to those on the outside, the black hole does not even exist yet, no matter how long they wait. Whereas for those on the inside, the black hole is the ONLY thing that exists, and its fate is sealed: soon enough everything, including time itself (!) comes to an end in this doomed mini-universe.

Text: What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? Intelligence has nothing to do with it. “Classical” has a lot to do with it. Let me explain. A “classical” entity: a human, a cat, a brick, a video camera, has well-defined states. A brick is either on the table or on the floor, never both. A human is either moving or standing still, never both. A cat is either alive or dead, never both. (Putting aside pointless philosophical musings about cats being, after all, “quantum” since they consist of a very large but finite number of uncorrelated quantum degrees of freedom… true, but for all practical intents and purposes, bricks, cats, etc., are classical. Any quantum behavior is averaged out to the extent that it vanishes.) A “quantum” entity is different. A quantum entity does not have a classically defined position or momentum. Rather, it has a state. That state, which may be described (depending on your mathematical preference) by a vector in an abstract space, or by a fancy wavefunction, can be used to calculate the probability of finding that quantum entity with a certain value for its position or momentum when it interacts with something classical. Let me explain how. What the equations actually tell us is that the state of the quantum entity evolves such that it is constrained by its past, present, and future interactions, including interactions with classical things such as bricks, cats or humans. Quantum physics is manifestly nonlocal (this is the essence of Bell’s famous theorem) so it is subject to constraints that can be arbitrarily far in space or time, yet curiously, somewhat counterintuitively, it remains causal (it is not possible to arrange the future to induce an observable influence on the past). A quantum entity is neither a particle nor a wave, it just displays behaviors of both under the right circumstances. The state of that quantum entity obeys a wave equation including the ability to exhibit interference patterns. But when a quantum entity interacts with a classical thing, the interaction may be localized, creating the appearance of something resembling a miniature cannonball, i.e., a particle. Concerning the double-slit experiment, the quantum entity may be a photon or an electron (so let me just call it an electron from now on), which is confined by three things: a) the location and time of emission; b) the slits; and c) the location and time of detection. These are the constraints that determine the wavefunction that characterizes this electron’s state. One possible interpretation, obviously inspired by the uncomfortable consequence of quantum nonlocality, namely that the location and time of detection is one of the constraints characterizing the system, is to take that constraint out of the picture initially. We then describe the state of an electron that is characterized by the location and time of emission, and the presence of the slits. The resulting wavefunction can be used as a probability amplitude, characterizing the probabilities of possible locations and times for the electron’s detection. When we actually do detect the electron, the picture changes: We now have a new wavefunction that is also constrained by the location and time of detection. This rather abrupt replacement of one wavefunction with another we call “wavefunction collapse”. Now it is true that this interpretation requires an intelligent creature, such as a human who prefers this probabilistic interpretation (the Copenhagen interpretation). But apart from some (not generally accepted) extensions of the quantum theory that treat wavefunction collapse as a physical process, the collapse is only a clumsy mental aid. It is a philosophical musing, not physical reality. In reality, that electron was always governed by a wavefunction subject to nonlocal constraints (again I stress, this is the fundamental essence of Bell’s theorem.) So to sum up, a quantum entity (photon, electron, etc.) is neither a particle nor a wave; its state is governed by a wave equation so it sometimes exhibits the consequences of wave-like behavior; its interactions may be highly localized, giving the impression of a particle; and intelligent observers have nothing to do with this unless we buy into the controversial concept of objective collapse (of the wavefunction), and perhaps not even then. Text: Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? Not sure if I’d call it a coincidence, nor is it, strictly speaking, true. Yes, the Higgs mechanism is responsible for the rest masses of all charged fermions (charged leptons and quarks). Why not neutrinos? Well, neutrinos need a different mechanism that yields the so-called mass mixing matrix, which is the secret behind the observed neutrino flavor oscillations. The Higgs mechanism is also responsible (albeit in a different way) for the masses of the electroweak vector bosons, but here, we have both the charged W-bosons and the neutral Z-boson. So there, there’s a particle that is massive thanks to the Higgs but has no electric charge. So perhaps a pertinent question is not so much why the Higgs prefers charged particles (since most elementary particles are charged) but why neutrinos have such weird behavior when it comes to mass. Text: Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the “electron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon”. That “virtual electron-positron pair” is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist’s mind. It is called “ virtual” because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac’s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn’t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the “Dirac sea” business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states “filled in”, unless a particle is missing, and it’s this “hole” that Dirac’s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac’s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac’s equation described them. "Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the \u201celectron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon\u201d. That \u201cvirtual electron-positron pair\u201d is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist\u2019s mind. It is called \u201c virtual\u201d because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac\u2019s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn\u2019t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the \u201cDirac sea\u201d business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states \u201cfilled in\u201d, unless a particle is missing, and it\u2019s this \u201chole\u201d that Dirac\u2019s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac\u2019s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac\u2019s equation described them. Text: In 3 dimensions, Cartesian coordinate systems are distinguishable from their mirror images. What is the situation in 3+1 dimensions and how many inequivalent images are there? Spacetime, with its three spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension, has two “mirror” symmetries: parity and time reversal. Parity is what you get when you look at things in a mirror. Time reversal is what you get when you play the movie backwards, so to speak. These things become important in particle physics. Most of our laws of physics remain unchanged under a parity transformation: You cannot tell if you are watching an actual physics experiment or its mirror image, as they both obey the same set of equations. But there are some exceptions; e.g., neutrinos and their mirror images are not equivalent. Similarly, most of the laws of physics are the same under time reversal: When we look at particle interactions, for instance, you cannot tell if the movie is being played normally or backwards, as the same equations apply in both cases. But again, there are subtle exceptions. An important result is that when we simultaneously form a mirror image, play the movie backwards, and replace particles with antiparticles, the results are indistinguishable from reality. The laws of nature are invariant under a CPT (charge-parity-time) transformation. But what about thermodynamics, you might wonder? Entropy picks a direction of time that cannot be reversed! True. But the underlying laws of nature are still CPT symmetric. What sets the direction of entropy are initial or boundary conditions. If we set up a physical system in a low entropy initial state and leave its final state unconstrained, it will evolve from low to high entropy, even though the laws governing any individual particle are symmetric under time reversal. As far as we know, the early state of our own universe was such a low entropy state, and the future of our universe is unconstrained. Hence, we have an “arrow of time” despite the fact that physics is governed by fundamental laws that are invariant under a CPT transformation. Text: When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet? We don’t observe particles. We observe specific properties of particles when we measure them. In an idealized measurement, when we measure a particle position for instance, it means we ensure that the particle interacts with a classical instrument that confines the particle’s position to a specific number (an eigenvalue). Consequently its momentum is completely unconfined. In a real measurement, our measuring instrument itself is made up of particles, so it’s not a purely classical instrument. Therefore, it does not perfectly confine the particle position to a number. Interpreting the particle’s state as a probability amplitude, it indeed means that, as per our measurement, we have something like a Gaussian probability distribution characterizing the particle’s position (or whatever property it was that was being measured).

Text: Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? Oh, in quantum mechanics, a particle like an electron is always a particle, an actual, immutable particle. The waves (which is to say, the wavefunction) determine the physical properties, including the position and momentum of this particle. In the Copenhagen interpretation, this wavefunction is interpreted as a probability amplitude, and it is used in conjunction with the concept of an idealized, classical measurement apparatus, to compute the probability of finding the electron somewhere, or moving with some momentum. In quantum field theory, there are no particles, only fields. The fields are quantum fields, which is to say, just like the position of that poor electron in quantum mechanics, the field does not have definite values at specific places and times; rather, a wavefunction determines (at least in the Copenhagen interpretation) the probability of finding the field with specific values at specific places and times. However, another property of these quantum fields is that when they interact, their values go up or down one unit at a time. It is these unit excitations that we observe, in localized interactions, with particle-like behavior. So to sum up/reiterate, in quantum field theory, an electron is an excitation of the corresponding fermionic field (the electron field). The wavefunction (not to be confused with the field proper) may be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probabilities of finding the field in a definite state using a classical instrument. Interactions between fields create and destroy excitations (“particles”). In contrast, in quantum mechanics particles are eternal, there are no fields, and the wavefunction can be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probability of finding the particle in some state somewhere using a classical instrument. Text: Does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? Quantum mechanics says nothing about determinism. In its canonical form, by way of Schrödinger’s equation, it simply tells you how a particular mathematical entity, namely the wavefunction, representing the state of the system, evolves. Interpretations of quantum mechanics, on the other hand, are a different story. The most popular “Copenhagen” interpretation of quantum mechanics treats the wavefunction as a probability amplitude. The interpretation introduces the concept of a “measurement” (an act that is not described by quantum mechanics itself) that replaces the state of the system with an “eigenstate”, one of the many possible outcomes of that measurement. The wavefunction can be used to compute the probabilities associated with the various outcomes. If this “collapse of the wavefunction” really happens (so-called “objective collapse”) that would make the physics nondeterministic. The present state of the system only determines the probabilities of the various possible outcomes of the measurement. But before we conclude that “objective collapse” is the way to go, I’d advise caution. This whole “collapse” business is introduced for reasons that are philosophical, not physical. What the physics (the math, actually) tells us is a different story. The full present state of the system is not knowable on the basis of classical observables. Quantities that characterize the present state cannot be localized in space or time. This implies that some of these “hidden” properties of the system may, in fact, be constrained by future events. Seemingly paradoxically, this does not actually violate causality: Despite being fundamentally nonlocal, the quantum theory (at least in the form of quantum field theory) cannot be used to send signals from the future to the past. Nonetheless, this nonlocal business is disturbing. It is resolved if we assume that no, the future does not constrain the present, rather, the actual future happens because the act of measurement causes the system to collapse! (Again, objective collapse.) Unfortunately, that seems like a cure that is worse than the disease: This collapse has to happen simultaneously in the entire universe (after all, we replace one nonlocal description of the state of the system with a different one) including not just all locations but all times! OK, so what if we don’t go so far? Sure, “collapse” is a useful concept to deal with practical scenarios, e.g., when the instrument is obviously a macroscopic object (say, a cat) and its state is really never in doubt (no one has ever seen, or will ever see, a cat that is both alive and dead.) But then we have an important point to ponder: Sure, we use “collapse” as a practical tool, but we know that in reality, things really never collapse, and the wavefunction simply evolves towards a near-eigenstate because it is constrained by a future measurement. In other words, we’d be taking the nonlocality of quantum physics literally. In this case, we have a theory that is deterministic but nonlocal. Yet, in the form of quantum field theory, it would still be a theory that respects causality, with no faster-than-light or backwards-in-time influences, ever. I’m personally in favor of this viewpoint so my immediate reaction to the question is that yes, quantum physics is deterministic. I recognize though that there are many other popular interpretations, but in the end, all this interpretation business is firmly in the realm of philosophy, not physics: The equations are the same, the predictions are the same, the results of experiments are the same no matter what philosophical baggage we attach to them, mostly just to resolve the cognitive dissonance that the weirdness of the quantum world can produce in our minds. I typically avoid adding inane Quora AI-generated images showing blackboards with nonsensical scribbles… but this one has a cat, a cute cat to boot, and I am way too fond of cats. Not to mention that cats can be forgiven for producing nonsensical scribbles on blackboards, I guess. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Text: Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? A strange question but certainly not a silly one! First, a reminder. I used the “pops on the square” analogy to explain why light from a single instance of time (the moment of time confusingly called the “surface of last scattering” when the cosmic microwave background originated) is seen as continuous radiation. To recap: You are in a very, very, very large square, full of people as far as the eye can see and beyond. Something happens, say, a flash in the sky, and simultaneously, everyone claps once. But that is not what you hear. The moment it occurs, you hear clapping nearby. A second later, you hear the clapping from people roughly 1000 feet away beause sound travels at a finite speed. Sure, the sound diminishes with distance but there are also more people along a circle of 1000 feet in radius than nearby, so the total intensity doesn’t really diminish that much. At two seconds, you hear clapping from even more people at 2000 feet away. At 10 seconds, it’s the folks at 10,000 feet. And so on. If the square is infinitely large, the clapping never stops. This is why we continue seeing cosmic background radiation. Granted, it’s faster, but Just like sound, light also travels at a finite speed. Today, we see light (well, microwave radiation) from volumes of gas at 13.8 billion light years (light travel distance); tomorrow, we’ll see it from volumes of gas situated at 13.8 billion light years and one light day away. How does this relate to Olbers’s Paradox? The 19th century German astronomer Olbers asked a simple question: If space is infinite, and there are stars everywhere, no matter which direction we look in the sky, eventually that direction should terminate on the surface of some distant star. So why is the night sky dark? The answer, of course, is that we do not live in an eternal universe. The universe has a finite age. No matter what direction we look, eventually we run out of stars: the oldest star cannot be older than the universe itself, so beyond 13.8 billion light years, there are no more stars. Given the density of stars in the universe, that means that in most sky directions, we don’t see any stars at all. There is more to the story of course because in an expanding universe, distant stars are also dimmer as they are receding from us, but we don’t even need expansion to understand the key argument: Olbers’s paradox works only in an eternal universe. Back to my example of the clapping crowd in the square: It’s different. The folks in the crowd are not clapping continuously. The clapping is a single event. But you know what? Text: Is MOND a statistical artifact and how do new gravity models answer the question of dark matter any more accurately? MOND is an “artifact” alright, in the sense that it is something created by humans, but it is not statistical in nature. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton’s second law, purportedly to model the anomalous rotation curves of spiral galaxies. That’s all. Take F = m a , and replace it with something. A particular something that, in MOND’s case, does not even obey basic conservation laws. Unfortunately, MOND has become synonymous with a much broader, reasonably respectable area of research, modified gravity. In fact, it has become a straw man unfortunately: It’s easy to see how many different ways MOND can go wrong, and all too often, it is seen as a failure of modified gravity theories in general. A modified gravity theory has to do a bunch of things. For starters, its effects must be absent in the laboratory, and here in the solar system. Which is to say, the theory’s predictions for observations like precision orbit calculations, GPS data, lunar laser ranging, planetary radar ranging, the Shapiro delay, Cassini radio science, Viking radio science, must all produce the right results. For spiral galaxies, the theory must match the empirical predictions of the so-called Tully-Fisher law. For smaller systems, such as globular clusters, it still needs to produce velocity dispersions that obey Newtonian physics. On the other hand, for galaxy cluster dynamics, it must produce something that resembles the observed distribution of stellar mass, gas (X-ray emissions) and weak lensing. Last but not least, on the cosmological scale, the theory must accurately reproduce things like the matter power spectrum (the large-scale distribution of galaxies) or the angular (acoustic) power spectrum of the microwave background. MOND does almost none of the above. Which should come as no surprise: It is not a modified theory of gravitation. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton’s second law. It is, of course, possible to build a more respectable modified gravity theory, and people have been trying to do that utilizing a variety of approaches for many years, starting with Jordan-Brans-Dicke theory from more than 60 years ago (but anticipated a century ago by Eddington, who first introduced expressions that can be used to parameterize families of modified gravity theories.) Some of these theories have been falsified by data, including, among other things, the “multimessenger” (gravitational and electromagnetic) observations of neutron star mergers. Other theories, like, say, Mannheim’s conformal gravity or Moffat’s MOG theory*, remain in contention. More recently, these theories have gained a little bit of traction, in particular because of the persistent failure of attempted experiments aimed at detecting dark matter directly. But the bar is set very high for modified gravity. It is insanely hard to produce a theory that successfully deals with all of the challenges that I listed above. Which is why the standard, “Lambda-CDM” model remains the leading contender, despite challenges such as the failure to detect dark matter, or contradictory results like the famed “Hubble tension” or the unexpected number of early mature galaxies seen by the JWST. But none of this has anything to do with MOND. MOND is just a silly phenomenological formula, that works for (some) spiral galaxies and does nothing else. It should not be treated as a straw man for modified gravity. *Disclaimer: I worked with Moffat on the MOG theory extensively over the past 20 years. "Is MOND a statistical artifact and how do new gravity models answer the question of dark matter any more accurately? MOND is an \u201cartifact\u201d alright, in the sense that it is something created by humans, but it is not statistical in nature. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton\u2019s second law, purportedly to model the anomalous rotation curves of spiral galaxies. That\u2019s all. Take F = m a , and replace it with something. A particular something that, in MOND\u2019s case, does not even obey basic conservation laws. Unfortunately, MOND has become synonymous with a much broader, reasonably respectable area of research, modified gravity. In fact, it has become a straw man unfortunately: It\u2019s easy to see how many different ways MOND can go wrong, and all too often, it is seen as a failure of modified gravity theories in general. A modified gravity theory has to do a bunch of things. For starters, its effects must be absent in the laboratory, and here in the solar system. Which is to say, the theory\u2019s predictions for observations like precision orbit calculations, GPS data, lunar laser ranging, planetary radar ranging, the Shapiro delay, Cassini radio science, Viking radio science, must all produce the right results. For spiral galaxies, the theory must match the empirical predictions of the so-called Tully-Fisher law. For smaller systems, such as globular clusters, it still needs to produce velocity dispersions that obey Newtonian physics. On the other hand, for galaxy cluster dynamics, it must produce something that resembles the observed distribution of stellar mass, gas (X-ray emissions) and weak lensing. Last but not least, on the cosmological scale, the theory must accurately reproduce things like the matter power spectrum (the large-scale distribution of galaxies) or the angular (acoustic) power spectrum of the microwave background. MOND does almost none of the above. Which should come as no surprise: It is not a modified theory of gravitation. It is an ad hoc modification of Newton\u2019s second law. It is, of course, possible to build a more respectable modified gravity theory, and people have been trying to do that utilizing a variety of approaches for many years, starting with Jordan-Brans-Dicke theory from more than 60 years ago (but anticipated a century ago by Eddington, who first introduced expressions that can be used to parameterize families of modified gravity theories.) Some of these theories have been falsified by data, including, among other things, the \u201cmultimessenger\u201d (gravitational and electromagnetic) observations of neutron star mergers. Other theories, like, say, Mannheim\u2019s conformal gravity or Moffat\u2019s MOG theory*, remain in contention. More recently, these theories have gained a little bit of traction, in particular because of the persistent failure of attempted experiments aimed at detecting dark matter directly. But the bar is set very high for modified gravity. It is insanely hard to produce a theory that successfully deals with all of the challenges that I listed above. Which is why the standard, \u201cLambda-CDM\u201d model remains the leading contender, despite challenges such as the failure to detect dark matter, or contradictory results like the famed \u201cHubble tension\u201d or the unexpected number of early mature galaxies seen by the JWST. But none of this has anything to do with MOND. MOND is just a silly phenomenological formula, that works for (some) spiral galaxies and does nothing else. It should not be treated as a straw man for modified gravity. *Disclaimer: I worked with Moffat on the MOG theory extensively over the past 20 years. Text: What would it look like to see a planet go through a wormhole as an observer? Poor wormholes. So badly misunderstood. First of all, even though they exist as legitimate solutions of Einstein’s field equations, these solutions almost certainly do not represent real physics. A stable wormhole? Even if it is possible to “construct” one (by “construct”, I mean in the mathematical sense, with pencil and paper, using equations), their existence is subject to a great many conditions, many of which are likely unphysical, which preclude their existence in the actual, physical, universe. But putting that aside… A wormhole that is large enough to swallow a planet without ripping it to shreds first due to differential (tidal) gravity would need to have a mass in the many ten billion solar mass range. And even then, the planet would not go through unscathed; the tidal forces may not be large enough to rip it apart, but they’d certainly be large enough to disrupt it completely. To avoid that, the wormhole would need to be even bigger, maybe in the several trillion solar mass category? But now we’re talking about a wormhole with a Schwarzschild radius measured in light years. To watch a planet approach, and go through, such a wormhole at a feasible velocity… might take thousands of years or more! So no, don’t expect to see planets traversing wormholes, except in badly written science-fiction series where gigantic wormholes are needed to plug gigantic plot holes. Text: Hypothetically, if you were carrying a torch and you entered the black hole and switched it on, then what would you see? Nothing special, actually. For the sake of this thought experiment, allow me to assume that the black hole is a) a supermassive black hole (so that tidal forces don’t kill you at its event horizon, and you can live longer than mere milliseconds after reaching the horizon), b) fully formed (an actual, physical black hole is always in the process of formation insofar as external observers are concerned; as an infalling observer, you’d be witnessing that formation, i.e., you’d be surrounded by all the matter and radiation ever consumed by that black hole), c) it’s in an otherwise empty universe (so we don’t have to worry about, e.g., you being killed by starlight blueshifted into hard X-rays as you fall deeper in the black hole’s gravity well even before hitting the horizon) and d) there is no Hawking radiation or other semiclassical effects… So really, just a purely geometric black hole, Schwarzschild’s vacuum solution in other words, with a mass parameter large enough to be survivable at least for a few seconds. What would you see? Absolutely nothing. Before or after the horizon, you are still in empty space. Your torch will reveal nothing. In fact, without detailed calculations, you would not even know when you crossed the horizon; to you, everything would continue to appear normal in your vicinity, just like before. If you are freely falling, just wearing a spacesuit, you’d feel like floating in empty space. No change when crossing the horizon. If you’re inside a spaceship, everything would appear perfectly ordinary. If you were eating your dinner while falling through the horizon, you’d be taking your next bite, oblivious to the fact that you just crossed the horizon. Your fate, of course, would be sealed. Once you cross the horizon, you are irreversibly cut off from the rest of the universe. Anything that ever fell, anything that ever will fall into the black hole is there with you, forming a collapsing “mini-universe”. Though you may be moving relative to the bulk of matter around you, an observation would reveal that you are, in fact, in a universe not unlike the “big” universe out there, described by similar equations (the Friedmann equations), but unlike the “big” universe, which is expanding, yours is collapsing, shrinking. Text: If not wearing your seatbelt was a choice instead of law, would you buckle up or go without? As a driver? Absolutely, I’d use my seatbelt. I’ve been in accidents. (Fortunately none involving personal injury to anyone). Therefore, I know both from theory and from practice what it means when the seatbelt not only keeps you safer (which you may not care about) but keeps you behind the wheel. Which means that if, after the accident, the vehicle is still (somewhat) controllable, you might regain control. You may be able to stop the vehicle before it causes additional harm to others. You may still be able to steer, preventing injury to others. All this is kind of hard to do if you have already left the vehicle through the windshield as a wingless projectile, or ended up on the rear seat as the vehicle spun about. Questions like this remind me of questions I sometimes see concerning religion: “If you are an atheist, what stops you from committing certain sins?” Here are a few words or phrases to contemplate: “Empathy”. “Compassion”. “Social responsibility”. In other words, even if you don’t care about your own safety in an accident, you could still consider that a seat belt might help you keep others, including quite possibly your own loved ones in that vehicle, safer. I know, I know, outlandish commie propaganda and all but hey, even Ayn Rand advocated enlightened self-interest: that is to say, the recognition that even if your own well-being takes precedence over that of the others, acting at least occasionally in the interests of the group might actually be beneficial to the individual…

Text: What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? Such an old question, yet without a decent answer! The mass in F = m a refers to inertial mass. Inertia characterizes a body’s resistance to a force. You can see how when you divide this equation throughout by the mass m : a = F / m . Which is to say that given a force, a body’s resulting acceleration is proportional to that force, but inversely proportional to the body’s mass. The greater the mass, the smaller the acceleration: a body with more mass has more inertia, more resistance to motion. The term “rest mass” is synonymous with inertial mass. Consider, in fact, the title of Einstein’s famous 1905 E = m c 2 paper, which reads in English: Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content? This paper establishes the equivalence of energy-content and inertia(l mass). The term “rest mass” means the same as inertial mass. It came into usage along with another term, “relativistic mass”, which combines the inertial mass of a body (which is an intrinsic property) and its kinetic energy (which is observer-dependent). Fortunately this concept is not much used anymore as it is grossly misleading and has been the source of much confusion. I am guessing that “variable mass” in the question may have referred to this relativistic mass. Gravitational mass measures how a body interacts with the gravitational field. According to the weak equivalence principle, gravitational mass and inertial mass are identical. This is what allowed Einstein to generalize his original relativity theory (now called special relativity) and extend it to become a field theory of gravitation. A theory that treats inertial and accelerating reference frames the same way (Einstein’s original objective) naturally becomes a theory of gravitation when the reference frame associated with falling in a gravitational field does not depend on the material properties of the falling object. So to sum up, the mass m in F = m a is inertial mass; it is the same as rest mass; thanks to the weak equivalence principle, it’s the same as gravitational mass; as to the concept of variable (relativistic) mass, the best advice I can offer is to forget you ever heard about such a thing. Text: The universe is 13.8 billion years old. But the fraction we are permitted to observe has an approximate radius of 47 billion light years. So, is space-time structure continuously expanding? Or, does it happen an inflationary era after the Big Bang? The problem here is that “distance” may not mean what you think it means in an expanding universe. Indeed, the most distant parts of the universe that we are able to observe would be “presently” at roughly 47 billion light years from here. But we are not observing them at the “present”. We are observing them as they were 13.8 billion years ago, when they were much closer to us. In fact, much closer than 13.8 billion light years but that, too, is misleading; the average gravity of the universe back then was much stronger, which means substantial gravitational time dilation (the main reason for cosmological redshift for very distant objects) so from our perspective, light from these things was moving much slower, too. In cosmology textbooks, you will find a variety of distance measures. The 47 billion light years figure is simply the coordinate distance in so-called “comoving coordinates” of these things from us. It has no direct physical meaning. There are other distance measures, like “luminosity distance” (how faint something is compared to its brightness at a known distance) or “angular diameter distance” (how small something appears in the sky compared to its apparent size at a known distance). And yes, “light travel distance”, which, unsurprisingly, is exactly 13.8 billion light years for an object from which it took 13.8 billion years for light to reach us. Finally, yes, the universe continues to expand, but no, it’s not “space-time structure”. It is things. Clusters of galaxies flying away from each other, the distance between them increasing, their density decreasing over time. Do not confuse this with the hypothetical concept of inflation: that represent a brief but significant period in the history of the very early universe, when things were pushed away from each other by repulsive gravity (present due to some hypothetical field that, much like a cosmological constant or a “dark energy” component, produces gravitational repulsion due to its negative pressure), accelerating the rate of expansion. This era supposedly ended when the universe was still very young, but that does not mean expansion stopped; it simply means that expansion, from this point onward, began to slow because attractive gravity is trying to pull things back together. More recently in the standard cosmological model, repulsion again took over because of the presence, and now dominance, of dark energy so for the past 5 billion years or so, the rate of expansion has been increasing; at least this is what we appear to deduce from observations of distant supernovae, supported by the “standard”, so-called Lambda-CDM, cosmological model. Text: Why a free isolated electon cant fully absorb a photon? It has to do with conservation laws. A photon’s energy and momentum are proportional to one another: E = p c . Now look at an interaction involving an electron absorbing a photon. Specifically, look at it from the coordinate reference frame in which the electron’s direction of motion changes but its speed remains the same. This means that there is a change in momentum (a vector quantity, which changes if its direction changes even if its magnitude remains the same) but no corresponding change in energy (the electron’s energy in this reference frame is the same before and after the absorption event.) This is a contradiction: it means that the electron absorbed zero energy but nonzero momentum, which is incompatible with the nature of a photon. (Similar reasoning also applies to electron-positron annihilation, explaining why, as a minimum, two photons must be produced in such interactions.) Now if the photon is not confined to the “mass shell”, things are different. Such photons do not exist as actual particles: they are “virtual particles”, essentially mathematical mnemonic devices that help us describe particle interactions. But these “virtual photons” do not obey the relationship, E = p c , therefore it is perfectly valid to speak of their emission or absorption by electrons, so long as we never forget that “virtual” literally means not real, i.e., we are talking about a computational bookkeeping device, not a physical particle. Text: **Question for a physicist: ** How are stars born according to the general theory of relativity? The general theory of relativity has very little to do with it, since stellar birth does not involve gravitational fields that come even close to being relativistic. So insofar as stellar births are concerned, Newtonian gravity will do just fine. The basic idea is this: When you have a cloud of stuff with minor density fluctuations, under the influence of gravity those fluctuations tend to grow over time. Where matter was denser to begin with, there’s more gravity, attracting more matter. Where matter was less dense to begin with, there’s less gravity and slower attraction. When the stuff is normal matter, say, mostly hydrogen, however, atoms and molecules eventually begin to collide. The infall becomes more randomized, kinetic energy turning into heat as atoms and molecules bounce off each other. It also means rising pressure, which will slow down the density growth. And that loss of kinetic energy to heat, which is radiated away? It means that stuff, once together, sticks together, having lost some or all of its kinetic energy that’d be needed for it to fly apart again. Continue the process for a while, and deep in the interior of the hydrogen cloud eventually the pressure and temperature become high enough for fusion. That is to say, hydrogen atoms will collide often enough, and powerfully enough, to occasionally fuse together. When that happens, a lot of energy is released in the form of high-speed particles like gamma ray photons, which then bounce into other things, transferring their kinetic energy, heating things up. Ultimately that heat escapes the cloud; viewed from the outside, the cloud begins to warm up, begins the glow, even as it continues to contract. Eventually, it settles down to an equilibrium between gravity and pressure. Meanwhile, its glow, its radiation, helps sweep away some of the leftover gas that did coalesce with the rest. What you’re left with is a fairly dense ball of gas, in the interior of which now nuclear fusion takes place at a steady rate. Not very fast, mind you; if the mass of the cloud is that of our Sun, chances are it’s producing no more heat per unit volume than a well-maintained compost pile. Except that it can continue doing that for billions of years. And that’s how a star is born. General relativity? The role it plays is minuscule, a tiny, tiny modification of Newtonian gravity. A few parts in a million, tops. Mind you, if that star is heavier, eventually it might collapse into an object with gravity so strong, general relativity can no longer be ignored, rather, it plays a major role. That would be a neutron star. However, that state comes at the end, not the beginning, of a star’s life cycle. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.
