Text: Is it fair to say that there is the equivalent of infinite acceleration at the event horizon of a black hole? Yes, it is fair to say that there is infinite acceleration at the event horizon, but it requires a qualifier: We first need to decide what we mean by acceleration in this context. If you were to watch an object fall into a black hole, you’d see the following: As the object approaches the horizon, anything and everything will appear to slow down from your perspective. The object would become invisible as a matter of fact because all signals coming from it would be subject to exponentially increasing redshift, making those signals effectively undetectable. But assuming that nonetheless, you can continue to track the object’s motion, you’d find that it never actually reaches the horizon: From your perspective, its motion will appear to freeze, the moment of it reaching the horizon (indeed, the moment the horizon itself forms in the first place!) forever remaining in your future. If you were to fall freely into a black hole, you would of course feel no acceleration. You might feel tidal forces because different parts of your body would try to follow different trajectories: If the black hole is small (and by “small”, I mean any size smaller than the largest supermassive black holes) these tidal forces would in fact rip your body to shreds. But if the black hole is large enough, you might survive reaching, and getting past, the horizon (ignoring quantum behavior here and the role played by Hawking radiation). And at no point would you feel acceleration: you would be in free fall all this time. However! Suppose you are testing your Almost Infinitely Powerful Rocket (tm), by trying to hover as close to the event horizon as possible. You will find that the closer you are to the event horizon, the more force you need to stay in position. In fact, soon enough you’d be quashed inside your rocket, so perhaps it might be wise to just send an unmanned probe instead. The bottom line: you will find that no matter how powerful your rocket it, there’s a point near the event horizon where it’s just not powerful enough to stay hovering. At the event horizon proper, the rocket would need to be infinitely powerful, i.e., subjected to infinite acceleration, in order to stay motionless, and that, of course, is impossible. So yes, as I said, it is fair to say that there is infinite acceleration at the event horizon: It would take an Infinitely Powerful Rocket (which cannot exist) to overcome gravity at the horizon proper and just hover.

Text: If all of the mass energy of colliding black holes is contained within their event horizons, how does the collision release any energy? Stuff can escape from the event horizon if it collides with another? But all the mass-energy of colliding black holes is not contained within their event horizons. You forgot about gravitational potential energy between the two black holes. Gravitational potential energy is zero when the black holes are very far apart, not interacting. As they get closer, that gravitational potential energy, which is negative (!), increases in magnitude. Since energy is conserved, this increase in negative potential energy must be accompanied by a corresponding increase in something positive. In this case, that something positive is the kinetic energy of the black holes accelerating towards each other. Now if the black holes were to collide head-on, this would be the end of the story: after the collision, the merged black hole would absorb all that kinetic energy. The total mass-energy of the system would be the same as before the collision: the sum of the masses of the progenitor black holes. But if the black holes approach each other off-center, they don’t collide right away. Rather, they will enter inspiraling orbits. This will produce gravitational radiation. The energy of that gravitational radiation will come at the expense of the kinetic energies of the inspiraling black holes. Now you’d think that would slow them down but orbital mechanics is tricky: as they lose energy, they enter into an ever tighter orbit, actually speeding up! This runaway process results in a gradual increase of the rate at which gravitational radiation is produced, reaching a final crescendo as the black holes get close enough to merge. Once the merger begins, the process rapidly comes to an end: a short “ringdown” phase occurs and the merger is complete. But in the meantime, a substantial amount of that gravitational potential energy, turned kinetic energy, is released as gravitational radiation and never becomes part of the mass-energy of the merged black hole. And in case you are wondering about actual, physical black holes that never quite reach the stage (as seen by us, outside observers) of forming actual event horizons, that makes no difference: though the respective event horizons remain forever in our future, the “asymptotic” behavior of the black holes is observationally indistinguishable from that hypothetical end state. Long story short: gravitational potential energy turns into kinetic energy that — in case of an off-center approach — turns into gravitational radiation before the merger is complete. Text: How do quarks give rise to the mass of protons and neutrons? As you know, the inertial rest mass of a thing is determined by its internal energy-content. This applies to everything: planets, humans, protons and neutrons. So how does this work considering that baryons (protons and neutrons) are made of triplets of quarks? First, the quarks have rest mass. (This rest mass it itself a result of an interaction between the quarks and the so-called vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field.) The rest masses of the constituent quarks about to roughly 1% of the rest masses of protons and neutrons. As for the rest, it’s the binding energy between those quarks. Think of the strong interaction (very crudely) as a force that’s like a tension spring. The tension spring is relaxed when it’s at its shortest. That’s when it has zero potential energy. When you stretch it, you invest work, add energy to the system. So think of those three quarks as being connected by tension springs. OK, things get a tad more complicated than that. First of all, a lot (and I mean a lot!) of energy is added to the system this way, so that means that as the springs do their thing, those quarks can start zipping around at high speed (though still safely inside the baryons). So a lot of the energy invested into the system is in the form of the kinetic energy of the quarks, not de facto tension in the springs themselves. Moreover, the tension in these springs is such that they can “snap”: in the case of the quark model, that means producing new ends for the spring fragments, which is to say, new quark-antiquark pairs. But these configurations are unstable, so the springs reconnect quickly, the quark-antiquark pairs vanish as quickly as they appear. The result is a soup, a continuous balance between potential energy, kinetic energy, virtual quark-antiquark pairs… but ultimately, as I said, it’s the binding energy between the three constituent quarks, whatever form it takes at any specific moment, that yields roughly 99% of the inertial rest mass of a proton or neutron. Text: If the “one-way” speed of light hasn’t yet been measured and we can just affirm the average 2-way speed of light for all points & perspectives is what measures c, what does that mean for ancient nighttime stars we see, that light’s not from long ago? Questions like this pop up regularly, and they are not silly. However, it is important to understand that ultimately, we do not measure speed, one-way, two-way or otherwise. We also do not measure distances. The only “pure” measurement that we can do without hidden assumptions is counting the ticks of a reliable clock. Of course even this measurement is based on an important assumption: Namely that in this universe, reliable clocks exist. Clocks that tick in sync; clocks that, when brought apart and later brought back together, will still continue to tick in sync (though they may have counted a different number of ticks in the meantime, while they were apart). All other measurements are derived from clock ticks. But… rulers! Oh, if idealized rulers existed… Well, then we wouldn’t have relativity theory, would we! An idealized ruler is perfectly rigid. Move one end and the other end moves instantaneously, no matter how far it is from the first! Spin the ruler at one end, and the other end will move around rapidly, perhaps many times faster than the vacuum speed of light! No such thing exists. Real rulers are physical objects, and when you move them around, different parts move at different speeds, depending on the material properties of the ruler, the speed of sound in that material and such things. In the end, the only way to properly calibrate a ruler is, you guessed it, by using a clever arrangement of reliable clocks and light signals. Yes, light signals. Because when two clocks are apart, we have no other means of relating their readings. So for instance, when we calibrate a ruler, we can attach a clock to one end, send a light signal to the other end and let it return, and then use the time elapsed on that clock to infer the length of the ruler. We can repeat this experiment using a clock on the other end, even a clock in the middle, but ultimately this is all we have: clocks and light signals. So we really have to turn things upside down. Forget about measuring the speed of light; assume that the vacuum speed of light is universal, then make a bunch of measurements, and check if the results are consistent with that assumption. They are. Of course you are free to propose alternatives. You are free to propose an alternative theory in which the speed of light is not constant, depends on direction, etc., and see if you can come up with results that are consistent with observation. However, unless your proposal is conceptually simpler than special relativity, do not be surprised if it is not received with enthusiasm. When two theories yield identical predictions, we generally prefer the one that’s simpler. And special relativity has a whole bunch of other factors supporting it, not the least the fact that Maxwell’s beautiful equations found a “native home” in four-dimensional spacetime, on account of the fact that the vacuum equations are conformally invariant in such a spacetime, and even in the presence of charges, the theory remains invariant under the Lorentz-Poincaré group. So for electromagnetism alone, special relativity is the native “playground”. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Text: A system composed by a piece of iron and a magnet has more energy if the iron is closer the magnet. So, the overall weight should be (very very slightly) different. Is there an intuitive thought experiment to show it? Actually, when you bring a piece of iron to a magnet, the system has less energy when the iron is closer to the magnet. You need to invest energy, do work to separate the iron from the magnet. The amount of energy is usually minuscule so it is not something we can measure, but to offer an intuition: Suppose you have a magnet and you release a piece of iron nearby. The magnet attracts it: the piece of iron accelerates, gaining kinetic energy at the expense of losing potential energy. The overall energy-content of the system remains the same.
